transcript.text: Is it normal for my dishwasher to leave everything wet? Plastic tubs are soaking every time and there's drips on the glasses. It's a Bosch Serie 4.

Plastic tubs staying wet is often normal, particularly on Eco or short programmes: plastic does not retain enough heat for condensation drying. Drips on glasses, though, usually point first to low rinse aid, a low rinse-aid setting, or a programme with limited drying rather than a failed part. 1. Check and top up the rinse-aid dispenser, then raise its setting one step if it is already full. Rinse aid helps water sheet off glasses instead of drying as droplets.
2. Try one full normal/intensive programme rather than Eco or Quick, and leave the door closed until the programme has fully ended. Once finished, opening it slightly can help; take care of the hot steam.
3. Avoid nesting cups and tubs or leaving them face-up where they can hold a pool of water. The key distinction is temperature: if everything is hot or steamy but wet, this is a drying/setting issue, not normally a heater fault. If glasses and crockery are cold as well as wet, especially if washing results have worsened, it could be a heating fault and would need further diagnosis.

Thanks. The rinse aid symbol is lit actually, so it's empty, I use all-in-one tablets. I always use Eco 50 and open the door straight away when it finishes. Everything's hot and steamy inside. Should I still top up the rinse aid?

Yes — top up the rinse aid even when using all-in-one tablets. The lit symbol means the machine is asking for it, and it is the most likely reason for the droplets on the glasses. Tablets may include a little rinse-aid agent, but it is often not enough for good drying, particularly on Eco 50. Your dishes being hot and steamy is reassuring: the dishwasher is heating, so this does not point to a heater fault. The remaining wetness is most likely normal Eco/condensation drying made worse by the empty rinse-aid reservoir. Plastic tubs will still tend to stay wetter than glass or china. 1. Fill the rinse-aid dispenser to the maximum mark, wiping up any spill. If there is a dose setting, leave it at its current setting initially; raise it one step only if glasses still have lots of droplets after a couple of washes.
2. For the next test, use a normal or intensive programme rather than Eco. This tells you how much is programme-related; Eco prioritises lower energy use and tends to leave more moisture behind.
3. Let the programme finish, then open the door slightly rather than fully straight away, taking care with the hot steam. Avoid cups and tubs facing upwards or nested together, as they will hold water regardless. If glasses and crockery are still very wet after rinse aid and a fuller programme, then the rinse-aid setting or loading is the next thing to adjust. Soaking plastic alone would still be broadly normal.

candidates: Rinse aid low or dose set too low (high)
Eco/Quick programme or passive condensation drying (high)
